name: gh-flow
description: One-shot issue-to-PR compositions: the ordinary chain, a spec-driven autopilot, dependency waves over a set of issues or the whole backlog, and a single-issue descendant wave.

interface.shortDescription: Carry a GitHub issue to a reviewed PR in one run
interface.longDescription: gh-flow owns the composition axis of the GitHub workflow: taking one issue all the way to a reviewed pull request in a single run, by chaining the atomic skills that live in the sibling repos. issue is the ordinary path - implement, commit, open the PR, run the review gate, then rebase-sync - and it stops dead at the first failing step with a resume hint rather than limping on. autopilot starts a step earlier, from an approved spec: it writes the plan, files the issue, implements, opens the PR, and answers review comments without asking for approval along the way, but it never merges - that stays a human decision. waves takes a set of issues whose order matters (by default every open issue, so it also sweeps a whole backlog): it plans dependency waves, runs each wave as one worktree and one background worker per issue, and verifies every wave live against the restarted app before re-planning the next. wave takes one issue instead: it carries it through issue and gh-pr:merge, re-verifies the merge commit in a fresh clone with gh-verify:merged, then processes only the open issues whose body marks them Spawned-from that issue, one at a time, capped by depth and count. All four are compositions, not reimplementations - each delegates to the atomic skill that owns the step, and none of them merges a PR by itself; the workers of waves and wave delegate that to gh-pr:merge, whose approval gates still apply (--no-merge on either merges nothing).
